INTRODUCTION. 


N this edition of the Index to Harrrr’s New Montuty Macazinr—em- 
bracing the contents of Volumes I.—LXX.—some new features have been 
introduced. 

To render the alphabetical sequence more conspicuous, all groups of titles 
under headings or names of authors have been set in nonpareil type, while the 
headings and names of authors appear in brevier antique. 

The Table of final pages in each Number, with the corresponding month 
and year, will be especially useful to those who have unbound sets. Thus, 
the Abbott Papyrus is mentioned in Volume LXV., page 195, which, on 
referring to the Table, is found to be in the July Number of 1882. 

The Editor's Historical Record has been inserted in complete form under 
the word “ Historical,” with a reference from the older title of “Current 
Events.” The Obituary Notices of the Historical Record, including over 
twelve hundred persons of note, appear in a separate list. 

The Index contains fifty-one thousand references. While the new material, 
referring to the last ten volumes (LXI.-LXX.), covers one-seventh of the 
Magazine text, the new matter introduced in the Index forms one-fifth of 
the present work, including a large number of new references to the earlier 
volumes not inserted in the previous editions. 

Each contribution appears under the author’s real name, under the title 
as given in the text, and under the subject or class heading. Where the 
authors are known by pseudonyms, cross-references are made from them to 
their real names; and where articles have obscure titles, they'are entered in 
other places—as, for example, the article “ First Families of the Atlantic” has 
references under the words Cod, Herring, and Mackerel ; “Mediterranean of 
the Pacific” under Puget Sound. , 

The entire literary matter of the Magazine has been arranged under the 
following Subject and General Headings:

INTRODUCTION. vii 





Illustrated articles are indicated by an asterisk, and in addition to this all 


the illustrations considered of permanent literary value have been indexed in 
the same manner as the reading-matter. This has been fully carried out, 
especially under such heads as Botany, Castles, Costumes, Paintings, Portraits, 
and Places. 

An elaborate system of over three hundred cross-references has been intro- 
duced to obviate the usual difficulties attending the compilation of a classified 
alphabetical work. The following will serve as types: Ballooning, see Aero- 
nautics. Cemeteries, see also Catacombs. Ethiopia, see Abyssinia. Prescott, 
Harriet E., see Spofford, Harriet P. Fine Arts, see also Ceramics, Engravings, 
Monuments, Music, Numismatics, Paintings, Portraits, Sculpture, and Statues. 

The Editorial Departments have been carefully analyzed. 1. The Ei/itor’s 
Historical Record contains notices of the leading historical and political events 
for the past thirty-five years, arranged chronologically. A glance at the Table 
of Contents of each Volume will give a view of the history of the period, with 
a reference to the page where each event is narrated. 2. The Editor's Easy 
Chair treats of current topics of a social and esthetic character, being entered 
under the head “ Chair, Editor’s Easy,” and distributed also throughout the 
Index. 3. The Editor's Scientific Record, supervised by Professor Spencer 
F. Baird, of the Smithsonian Institution, was introduced in Volume XL., and 
extends from January, 1870, to November, 1879. It embraces a review of the 
more recent discoveries in Science, and their applieation to the Arts. The 
indexing of this department has received special attention, and from its large 
number of cross-references will prove of service to readers interested in Science. 

The seventy Volumes of the Magazine constitute a very full Cyclopedia 
of Travel, Discovery, and Adventure, which the present revision aims to make 
thoroughly available by noting all important explorations and memorable 

voyages. This record, covering a period of thirty-five years, constitutes a very 
complete exposition of modern life in every department —literary, esthetic, 
social, and industrial—including, also, faithful descriptions of barbaric races 
and partially explored countries.
